new.title: Frame the Hoge der A from the Vissersbrug
new.desc: Old warehouses and merchant houses line this quiet canal, with the tower of the Der Aa-kerk rising behind them. It is the postcard view of old Groningen, and most visitors never wander this far west of the Grote Markt.
new.tip: Stand on the Vissersbrug for the classic shot, then walk the full length of both the Hoge and the Lage der A.

new.title: Visit John Hejduk's Wall House #2
new.desc: A strange, colourful house of separate rooms clinging to one concrete wall, designed in the 1970s by American architect John Hejduk and only built in 2001 on the shore of the Hoornse Meer. It is now looked after by the Groninger Museum.
new.tip: The inside is only open on weekends, often with a small exhibition; on other days the outside alone is worth the bike ride.

new.title: Wander the colourful Reitdiephaven
new.desc: A newer harbour neighbourhood where every house along the water has its own bright colour and shape. It feels like a seaside village tucked into the northwest of the city.
new.tip: Cycle out along the Reitdiep and combine it with a drink at Baxbier on the other side of the water.

new.title: Grab a terrace seat at De Drie Gezusters
new.desc: The big café on the corner of the Grote Markt is where Stadjers have been meeting for generations, from afternoon coffee to late-night beers. Its terrace looks straight at the Martinitoren.
new.tip: On a sunny afternoon go early; the terrace is full by the time classes and offices let out.

new.title: Find the hidden door of The Stockroom
new.desc: A cocktail bar hidden behind what looks like an ordinary storage room, styled after a 1920s speakeasy. Finding the entrance is half the fun.
new.tip: It is small, so reserve on weekend evenings.

new.title: Drink local beer by the Reitdiep at Baxbier
new.desc: Groningen's own craft brewery has a tasting room with a sunny terrace right on the Reitdiep. You drink the beer a few metres from where it is brewed.
new.tip: Ask for a tasting board of whatever is fresh from the tanks.

new.title: Have a beer at Kroeg van Klaas
new.desc: A brown neighbourhood pub in the Oosterpoort that has barely changed in almost fifty years, with live music and a terrace full of flowers. This is where the neighbourhood comes to talk.
new.tip: Pair it with a concert at De Oosterpoort around the corner.

new.title: Dine in an old grain silo
new.desc: De Graansilo serves a surprise menu inside a former grain silo, with a terrace over the Winschoterdiep. A reminder that this side of the city was once all industry and shipping.
new.tip: Book a table on the terrace on a summer evening to watch the boats go by.

new.title: Browse the Folkingestraat
new.desc: Once voted the nicest shopping street in the Netherlands, it is full of small boutiques, antique shops, galleries and cafés instead of chains. Spice shop Le Souk alone is worth the detour.
new.tip: Walk it from the Vismarkt end towards the station, and look out for the old synagogue along the way.

new.title: Walk the hidden hofjes route
new.desc: Groningen hides more courtyard almshouses (hofjes) than you would guess, each behind a modest door. A walking route links several of them into one quiet tour of the old centre.
new.tip: Pick up the hofjes route at the Groningen Store in the Forum; residents live in the courtyards, so keep your voice down.

new.title: Swim and watch the sunset at the Hoornseplas
new.desc: On warm days half the city cycles south to the Hoornsemeer to swim, sunbathe and stay for the sunset. The bigger Paterswoldsemeer next door is the place for sailing.
new.tip: Beachclub Kaap Hoorn on the shore is the spot for a drink with your feet in the sand; go on a weekday to avoid the crowds.

new.title: Lose an afternoon in the Stadspark
new.desc: The city's biggest park, just outside the ring road, has woods, meadows, ponds and a deer camp. It is where Stadjers go running, picnicking and to big summer events.
new.tip: It is an easy bike ride from the centre; bring a picnic, there is plenty of room to spread out.

new.title: Hang out at the Suikertuin and the city beach
new.desc: The old sugar factory grounds on the west side of the city have become a rough industrial playground with a festival terrace and a city beach next door.
new.tip: A good place to start a summer evening; check what is on, as the terrain hosts regular events.

new.title: See the tiles of the Princessehof in Leeuwarden
new.desc: Leeuwarden's ceramics museum fills a small 17th-century palace with tiles, Chinese porcelain and modern ceramics. M.C. Escher was born in the middle house of the building.
new.tip: The courtyard café is a lovely break; the Oldehove tower is a five-minute walk away.

new.title: Walk the old harbours of Harlingen
new.desc: Between the Noorderhaven and Zuiderhaven, gabled merchant houses from the 16th to 18th centuries look out on traditional sailing barges. Harlingen is still a working port with a fishing fleet and shipyard.
new.tip: Harlingen is the ferry port for Terschelling and Vlieland, so this makes a great stop before or after an island trip. Trains from Leeuwarden take about half an hour.

new.title: Discover painted Hindeloopen
new.desc: This tiny Elfsteden town on the IJsselmeer developed its own style of furniture painting, with flowers and curls on red, green or blue backgrounds, plus its own costumes. Cobbled lanes, wooden bridges and captains' houses complete the picture.
new.tip: Museum Hindeloopen shows the painting and costumes; the shops on the main street still sell painted pieces made in the old style.

new.title: Circle the ramparts of Dokkum
new.desc: The northernmost of the Eleven Cities still has its well-preserved bastions (bolwerken), crowned by two windmills, Zeldenrust and De Hoop. Saint Boniface was killed nearby in 754, and a chapel and park honour him.
new.tip: Walk the ring of the bolwerken, then visit the Bonifatius park. Buses run from Leeuwarden and Groningen.

new.title: Step back in time in Orvelte
new.desc: A car-free Drenthe village kept as a living monument of old farm architecture, with Saxon farmhouses, cobbled lanes and craftspeople at work. The Bruntingerhof is said to be the oldest surviving farm in Drenthe.
new.tip: Leave the car outside the village and take the horse-drawn tram; there is a market or event on many weekends.

new.title: Remember at Kamp Westerbork
new.desc: From this transit camp in Drenthe more than 100,000 Jews, Roma and Sinti were deported during the Second World War. The memorial of 102,000 stones and the bent rails on the camp site leave a lasting impression.
new.tip: Start at the memorial centre near Hooghalen, then walk or take the shuttle to the camp site; the giant radio telescopes stand right beside it.

new.title: Meet the Yde Girl at the Drents Museum in Assen
new.desc: Drenthe's main museum holds the Pesse canoe, the oldest boat ever found, and bog bodies such as the Yde Girl. It also stages big international exhibitions that draw visitors from all over the country.
new.tip: Assen is about 20 minutes by train from Groningen; the museum is a short walk from the station.

new.title: Visit the terp village of Garnwerd
new.desc: A small village on a man-made mound (wierde) beside the Reitdiep, with a church whose choir dates from 1229 and the 19th-century mill De Meeuw. It is one of the most atmospheric villages of the Groninger Ommeland.
new.tip: Cycle here from the city along the Reitdiep, or walk in on the Pieterpad, which passes through.

new.title: Find the little church of Oostum
new.desc: A 13th-century church on a mound in the flat countryside, painted again and again by the expressionists of De Ploeg. It is the Groningen landscape in one picture.
new.tip: It lies on stage 2 of the Pieterpad between Winsum and Groningen, a good walk or bike ride from the city.

new.title: Climb the striped lighthouse of Ameland
new.desc: The red-and-white Bornrif lighthouse near Hollum has stood since 1881 and is now a museum. From the balcony, after more than 230 steps, you see the whole island and on clear days its neighbours.
new.tip: Ferries to Ameland leave from Holwerd; rent a bike in Nes and cycle west to Hollum.

new.title: Eat poffertjes at Tante Til in Enumatil
new.desc: A charming coffee and tea house in the Westerkwartier, known for warm homemade poffertjes with butter and brown sugar. A favourite stop on a drive or ride west of the city.
new.tip: Combine it with the windmill in Noordhorn and the farm shop there on the way back.

new.title: Buy Frisian suikerbrood in Sneek
new.desc: Fries suikerbrood is a soft bread packed with pearl sugar and cinnamon, and it tastes best fresh from a Frisian bakery. Bakkerij De Haan in Sneek is a local favourite, and also bakes oranjekoek.
new.tip: Eat a slice with butter, then walk to the Waterpoort, Sneek's water gate.

new.title: Eat fresh fish in Lauwersoog harbour
new.desc: Lauwersoog is the fishing harbour at the edge of the Lauwersmeer national park, where the catch from the Wadden and North Sea comes in. The fish market by the boats is the place for a fresh lekkerbekje or kibbeling.
new.tip: Afterwards climb the dyke on the Strandweg for a 360 degree view over the sea and the national park.

new.title: Eat poffertjes at De Lickebaert on Vlieland
new.desc: On car-free Vlieland the pancake house De Lickebaert on the Dorpsstraat is the classic stop for a plate of fluffy poffertjes with powdered sugar.
new.tip: Ferries to Vlieland leave from Harlingen; everyone on the island gets around by bike.

new.title: Taste Terschelling cranberries
new.desc: Cranberries grow wild in Terschelling's wet dune valleys, supposedly since a barrel washed ashore in 1845. Islanders turn them into chutney, cordial, wine and sweets you will hardly find on the mainland.
new.tip: Look for cranberry products in the shops around the Torenstraat in West-Terschelling, and order cranberry juice or cake in the island cafés.

new.title: Roam the old prison of the Blokhuispoort in Leeuwarden
new.desc: Leeuwarden's former prison is now a cultural hub with the city library, studios, small shops, cafés and a hostel in the old cells. Walking its galleries and corridors is free.
new.tip: Spend the night at the Alibi Hostel if you want to sleep behind bars.

new.title: Watch kaatsen at the PC in Franeker
new.desc: Kaatsen is Friesland's own ball game, a kind of handball with tennis-like scoring. Its big tournament, the PC, has been played in Franeker since 1854 and calls itself the oldest regular sports tournament in the world.
new.tip: The whole town comes out for the PC in summer; check the date and combine it with the Eise Eisinga Planetarium.

new.title: Cheer on the skûtsjes on the Frisian lakes
new.desc: Every summer the old Frisian cargo sailing boats, the skûtsjes, race across the Frisian lakes in a series of regattas that draws crowds to the shores. Friesland is built around its lakes, and this is when they come alive.
new.tip: Ask a tourist office for the race calendar; around Sneek and Grou you can watch from the shore or from a spectator boat.

new.title: Hike the heath of the Dwingelderveld
new.desc: This Drenthe national park protects what is called the largest wet heathland in Western Europe, with fens, moorland and a flock of sheep keeping the heather short. In late summer the heath turns purple.
new.tip: Start at the visitor centre and follow the boardwalk routes; come in August or September for the blooming heather.

new.title: Stargaze in Lauwersmeer national park
new.desc: Lauwersmeer is one of the darkest places in the Netherlands and an official Dark Sky Park. Viewing platforms (hemelplatforms) such as the Vlinderbalg let you lie back under a sky full of stars.
new.tip: Pick a clear, moonless night, give your eyes twenty minutes to adjust and bring a blanket; it gets cold by the water.

new.title: Cycle between shows at Oerol on Terschelling
new.desc: For ten days every June the whole island becomes a stage, with theatre in the dunes, barns, bunkers and on the beach. The name comes from the island word for 'everywhere'.
new.tip: Book your bed months ahead and bring or rent a bike; much of the street theatre is free.

new.title: Ride the Vliehors Express on Vlieland
new.desc: A big off-road truck carries you across the Vliehors, a vast sand plain at the west end of Vlieland that feels like a desert. With luck you see seals on the way without getting on a boat.
new.tip: Tours leave from Het Posthuys; book ahead in summer.
